question: Do two milkweeds independently classified as high-performance monarch larval hosts have different adult-survival responses to predator-exposed versus cage treatments, including a possible host ranking reversal?
origin: Both Asclepias speciosa and A. fascicularis are H3 in Greenstein et al 2022 S1 Appendix; an independent 2018-2019 outdoor common-garden factorial source can test context dependence of actual adult eclosion.

source.publication_status: study already published host x predator effects on development, growth and adult morphology

original_data_vars.endpoint: survived_binary, adult eclosion from second instar placement

design.cohort: one larva per experimental plant per study year, n approximately 322+171
design.inclusion: valid host, treatment, binary survival, unique monarch_id; no dropping of exposed deaths
design.primary_effect: pooled year-weighted [cage-roof adult-emergence risk difference for As] minus same risk difference for Af
design.model: binomial GLM survived_binary ~ study_year + host + cage + host:cage, test 1-df interaction by likelihood-ratio
design.uncertainty: stratified nonparametric bootstrap within year x host x treatment cells; percentile 95% CI

secondary: within-year host x treatment interaction risk differences
whether host ranking crosses between cage and roof treatments, assessed descriptively
plants and fate missingness by year x condition
pupation and growth only as supporting endpoints if clearly linked
decision: Promote only if adult-survival interaction is supported, confidence interval excludes zero, direction consistent across 2018 and 2019, and result is not already the central published result. Otherwise label a mechanism-relevant negative or unresolved endpoint and stop.
qualifiers: Predator-exclusion cage can alter microclimate, so cage effects are not pure predation estimates.
Host genotype, plant architecture, and between-year effects may influence outcomes.
Two native milkweeds, not a cultivation-vs-naturalization origin contrast.
Existing 2026 paper already discusses host dependence of growth under predator exposure; the source reanalysis is not independent experimental replication.
Adult survival in common garden is not butterfly geographic distribution or fitness across global introduced regions.
